last_transition_reason: The proof correctly establishes the equivalence by reducing polynomiality of Q(q)=N(q)/D(q) to divisibility D|N, then characterizing divisibility over C[q] via root multiplicities. For a primitive n-th root of unity, each factor q^m-1 contributes multiplicity exactly 1 iff n divides m, so the multiplicities of N and D at such roots are precisely mu_n(A,d) and mu_n(B,d). This gives both directions, including the converse for arbitrary roots of D by passing to their order. The empty-product case d=0 is also covered. No semantic drift or illegal dependency use is present.
latest_nl_proof:
Let N(q):=prod_{i=1}^d (q^(A+i)-1) and D(q):=prod_{i=1}^d (q^(B+i)-1), with the empty product equal to 1 if d=0. Since (1-q^(A+i))/(1-q^(B+i))=(q^(A+i)-1)/(q^(B+i)-1) for each i, we have Q(q)=N(q)/D(q).

Because each factor q^(B+i)-1 is monic, D is monic. Hence Q(q) belongs to Q[q] if and only if D divides N in Q[q]. Also, because D is monic, D divides N in Q[q] if and only if D divides N in C[q]: the forward implication is obvious; for the reverse one, if N=DP with P in C[q], divide N by D in Q[q] to get N=DS+R with S,R in Q[q] and either R=0 or deg R<deg D. Then R=D(P-S). If R were nonzero, deg R would be at least deg D, contradiction. So R=0 and N=DS with S in Q[q].

For a complex number alpha and a nonzero polynomial F, write m_alpha(F) for the multiplicity of alpha as a root of F, and set m_alpha(F)=0 when alpha is not a root. By factorization into linear factors over C, D divides N in C[q] if and only if m_alpha(D) <= m_alpha(N) for every alpha in C.

Now fix a positive integer n and choose a primitive n-th root of unity zeta in C. For any integer m>=1, zeta is a root of q^m-1 exactly when n divides m. Moreover, when n divides m, that root is simple, because the derivative of q^m-1 is m q^(m-1), and m zeta^(m-1) != 0. Therefore m_zeta(q^m-1)=1 if n|m, and m_zeta(q^m-1)=0 otherwise.

Summing over the factors in N and D gives m_zeta(N)=#{i in {1,...,d} : n divides A+i}=mu_n(A,d), and similarly m_zeta(D)=#{i in {1,...,d} : n divides B+i}=mu_n(B,d).

Suppose first that Q(q) belongs to Q[q]. Then D divides N in Q[q], hence also in C[q]. So m_alpha(D) <= m_alpha(N) for every alpha in C. Applying this to a primitive n-th root zeta, and using the displayed formulas, gives mu_n(B,d) <= mu_n(A,d) for every positive integer n.

Conversely, assume mu_n(B,d) <= mu_n(A,d) for every positive integer n. Let alpha be any complex number. If alpha is not a root of D, then m_alpha(D)=0 <= m_alpha(N). If alpha is a root of D, then alpha^(B+i)=1 for some i, so alpha is a root of unity. Let n be the order of alpha. Then alpha is a primitive n-th root of unity, so by the formulas above m_alpha(D)=mu_n(B,d) <= mu_n(A,d)=m_alpha(N). Thus m_alpha(D) <= m_alpha(N) for every alpha in C. Hence D divides N in C[q], and therefore also in Q[q]. Consequently Q(q)=N(q)/D(q) belongs to Q[q].

Thus Q(q) is in Q[q] if and only if mu_n(B,d) <= mu_n(A,d) for every positive integer n, as claimed.
role_in_parent: Extracts a purely arithmetic consequence of the hypothesis that Q_{A,B,d}(q) is a polynomial.
statement_nl: Let A,B,d be integers with A >= B >= 0 and d >= 0, and define Q(q) := prod_{i=1}^d (1 - q^(A+i)) / (1 - q^(B+i)), with the empty product equal to 1 if d=0. For each positive integer n and each integer C, define mu_n(C,d) to be the number of indices i in {1,...,d} such that n divides C+i. Then Q(q) belongs to Q[q] if and only if mu_n(B,d) <= mu_n(A,d) for every positive integer n.

domain_restrictions: A,B,d are integers with A >= B >= 0
d is an integer with d >= 0
C ranges over all integers in the definition of mu_n(C,d)
In mu_n(C,d), the counting index i ranges over the set {1, ..., d}
If d = 0 then the set {1,...,d} is empty and the product defining Q(q) is the empty product, taken to be 1
statement_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For fixed integers A,B,d with A >= B >= 0 and d >= 0, define Q(q) as the product over i from 1 to d of (1 minus q to the power A plus i) divided by (1 minus q to the power B plus i), with the convention that when d = 0 this product equals 1. Then Q(q) is a polynomial in the indeterminate q with rational coefficients (that is, Q(q) belongs to Q[q]) if and only if for every positive integer n, the number of indices i in {1,...,d} satisfying n divides B plus i is at most the number of indices i in {1,...,d} satisfying n divides A plus i.
quantifier_order: Fix integers A,B,d with A >= B >= 0 and d >= 0
Define Q(q) using a product over i from 1 to d, with empty product equal to 1 when d = 0
Define mu_n(C,d) for every positive integer n and every integer C as the count of i in {1,...,d} such that n divides C+i
Claim: Q(q) is in Q[q] if and only if for every positive integer n, mu_n(B,d) <= mu_n(A,d)
